case_analysis.thread_summary: The thread focuses on how Bluetooth qualification requirements change when adding HID11 functionality to an existing qualified design under QPRDv3 Qualification Workspace. The discussion compares older PRDv2.3 Launch Studio behavior against newer Qualification Workspace interoperability testing behavior. The exchange also covers whether CTKD changes require requalification, how customer-run PTS testing can be used for qualification evidence, and how to handle incomplete HID11 PTS coverage. The consultant guides the customer through qualification scope determination, test planning, exported project validation, and evidence preparation.
case_analysis.key_technical_discussion: The consultant explains that CTKD does not appear as a separate ICS capability in SEC or LESEC and therefore enabling CTKD through application or Android layer changes alone does not automatically require a new qualification. A major discussion point is that QPRDv3 Qualification Workspace generates interoperability testing obligations based on the complete combined design, not only the newly added HID11 profile. The consultant clarifies that Include QDID registrations inherit IOPT obligations from referenced profiles, unlike older PRDv2.3 workflows. The thread also explains how exported .bqw project files, ICS data, generated test plans, and customer-generated PTS reports can be reviewed and accepted as qualification evidence. Finally, the consultant warns that HID11 PTS support may still have incomplete or member-defined coverage, requiring supplemental manual interoperability testing.
case_analysis.key_decision_logic: Qualification impact is determined by the final integrated design represented in Qualification Workspace and by whether implementation changes modify qualified Bluetooth protocol or profile behavior. If a change does not alter ICS-declared protocol functionality, existing qualification reuse may remain valid. Under QPRDv3, interoperability obligations are generated from the entire included design plus new additions, so inherited profiles can trigger additional mandatory IOPT cases. Qualification evidence is acceptable only when the exported project, ICS configuration, generated test plan, and executed test evidence all remain consistent with the declared design.
case_analysis.risk_if_done_wrong: If the customer assumes only the newly added HID11 profile requires testing, mandatory inherited IOPT cases may be missed, causing registration rejection, retesting, or qualification delays. Incorrectly assuming CTKD changes are always qualification-neutral could leave protocol-layer modifications unqualified. Failing to validate Qualification Workspace exports and ICS consistency can result in incomplete or invalid evidence submissions. Delayed identification of unsupported HID11 PTS cases can create unexpected manual interoperability testing work late in the project schedule.
case_analysis.consulting_mistake: An earlier assumption based on older PRDv2.3 Launch Studio behavior suggested that only newly added HID11-related interoperability testing would be required. This was later corrected after reviewing QPRDv3 Qualification Workspace behavior, which generates testing obligations from the full combined design including inherited referenced profiles. The correction highlights the importance of not applying deprecated Launch Studio qualification assumptions to Qualification Workspace registrations.
case_analysis.consulting_takeaway: Always determine Bluetooth qualification scope from the final integrated Qualification Workspace design and generated test plan rather than relying on historical workflow assumptions or incremental feature thinking. Verify ICS consistency, inherited profile obligations, and actual generated IOPT coverage early, especially when reusing existing QDIDs or adding newer profiles such as HID11.
